Where we are

Yesterday, in Class 7, we closed Topic 2. For the fictional company Ébénisterie Val-des-Pins Inc. you now have a network map, a list of monitoring needs, and an ordered monitoring plan that says which asset is observed first and how much data (2,275 MB (megabyte) per day) and how much technician time (60 minutes per day) the plan may consume. Lab 1 asks you to produce the same three documents for your own variation of that network; it is due on Sunday, October 11, 2026, at 23:59 EDT (Eastern Daylight Time), through the Léa DropBox.

Today we open Topic 3, Monitoring Tools, with two lessons: 3.1 Categories of monitoring tools and 3.2 Selecting the right tool for a given need. Both lessons are on the Midterm Exam of Thursday, October 1 — the outline says the exam covers Topics 1 to 3 "up to the selection of tools", which is exactly Lesson 3.2. Monday's Class 9 is the review class; next Friday (Class 11) we continue with 3.3 installing tools and applying updates and 3.4 creating the reference database; Saturday, October 3 (Class 12), we configure alerts and you start Lab 2, in which you install and configure the tool that today's second lesson teaches you to choose.

What you will be able to do after this class

  • Name the seven categories of monitoring tools, say what kind of evidence each one observes, how it collects that evidence, and where it is placed on a small network.
  • Classify any tool on six axes: agent-based or agentless, passive or active, continuous or scheduled, signature-based or baseline-based, open-source or commercial, on-premises or cloud.
  • Select a tool for a stated need with a repeatable procedure — need, constraints, long list, knock-out filter, weighted scoring, pilot, decision record — and justify the choice in writing.

These outcomes correspond to element 3 of competency EZ01 (the competency code: Monitor a computer network from a cybersecurity perspective), performance criterion 3.1, "appropriate selection of surveillance tools". The monitoring plan of Lab 1, the coverage map you build today, and the decision record of Lesson 3.2 are the three inputs of Lab 2.

The rule that governs every tool named today

This lecture names about twenty products. Every one of them is lawful to study, to download from its publisher's official site, and to run inside your Authorized Lab Environment — the VirtualBox laboratory you built in the Safe Lab Walkthrough. Every one of them is an offence to run against a network you do not own or are not authorized in writing to monitor. Section 7.2 of the Legal Notice adds the rules specific to this course: capture only on Designated Targets inside the lab; treat every capture, log file, baseline and alert record as personal information about the people who used those systems; never install an agent, sensor or collector on a device belonging to another person, an employer or the College; never enable promiscuous or monitor mode on a network you share with other people. Nothing is installed today. Today we learn to recognize the tools and to choose among them; installation begins in Class 11, in the lab, on Designated Targets only.

A note on the links in this document: every organization, standard and product is linked to its official site, and each link is followed by a small "VirusTotal check" link that opens the address in VirusTotal's search. Annex C of the Legal Notice asks you to read the address letter by letter and to scan it before you click; the habit is part of the profession, not a formality.

Lesson 3.1 · 30 minutes · Slides 7–37 of the deck

Categories of monitoring tools

3.1.1 What a monitoring tool is

A monitoring tool is a program, a device or a service that collects observations about a computer, a network device or a service, stores those observations, and presents or evaluates them. Every monitoring tool performs one or more of three functions. Collection is obtaining raw observations from a data source — an event log, a network interface, a counter inside a switch. Storage is keeping those observations for a defined period, the retention period, so that they can be searched later; Val-des-Pins chose 90 days in Class 7. Evaluation is comparing the observations with something — a rule, a threshold, a baseline of normal activity — and producing an alert when the comparison indicates a problem. Presentation is showing the observations to a person as a table, a graph or a dashboard. A tool that only collects and stores (a syslog server) is still a monitoring tool; a tool that only presents (a dashboard) is useless without the two others. When you evaluate a product, the first question is: which of the three functions does it perform, and on which data source?

Most tools are assembled from four kinds of components, and the same four words appear in every product's documentation. An agent is a small program installed on the monitored computer; it reads local data — event logs, running processes, files — and sends it to a central server. A sensor (also called a probe) is a device or a program connected to the network that reads the traffic passing by; nothing is installed on the monitored computers. A collector is the central program that receives what agents and sensors send, or that polls the devices itself, and writes the data to storage. A console (also called manager, server or dashboard) is the part the technician uses to search, to visualize and to receive alerts. When a product is described as agent-based or agentless, the statement concerns the first two components: whether something must be installed on the monitored machine, or whether the tool observes it from outside.

3.1.2 The five kinds of evidence, and why categories exist

Categories exist because each tool observes one kind of evidence, and the kinds differ in nature, in volume and in what they can prove. An event is a record that something happened at a given moment: a user logged on, a service stopped, a firewall rule was changed. Events are written into logs by operating systems, applications and network devices. A metric is a measured value sampled at regular intervals: processor load, free disk space, bytes per second on an interface, whether a device answered a ping. A flow record is the summary of one network conversation — source address, destination address, protocol, ports, start time, number of packets and bytes — without the content of the conversation. A packet is the complete unit of data transmitted on the network, including its content when the content is not encrypted. A state is the configuration, the installed versions or the list of known weaknesses of a system at one moment, obtained by inspecting the system.

Five kinds of evidence — events, metrics, flow records, packets and states — give the first five categories in the table below. Two more categories do not collect new evidence: they examine the evidence for signs of attack (intrusion detection) or combine all of it (correlation and alerting). Tools of the same category are largely interchangeable: choosing between them is the subject of Lesson 3.2. Tools of different categories are complementary: one does not replace the other, because they observe different evidence. This is why the monitoring needs of Class 6 were written with the data source in mind — "logon events on SRV-FILE-01", "connection records at FW-01" — each need points to a kind of evidence, and each kind of evidence points to a category.

3.1.3 The seven categories

Category 1 — Log collection and management tools (evidence: events)

On Windows, the operating system writes events to the Windows Event Log, organized in channels such as Security, System and Application; the Security channel records logons, logoffs, account changes and — only when the audit policy enables it — access to files and folders. On Linux and on most network devices (firewalls, switches, access points, NAS (Network-Attached Storage) appliances), events are written in the syslog format defined in RFC (Request for Comments) 5424, and the device can be configured to send each message over the network to a syslog server, historically on UDP (User Datagram Protocol) port 514 and, when the device supports it, encrypted with TLS (Transport Layer Security) on TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) port 6514. Windows can forward its events to a central computer with WEF (Windows Event Forwarding); more often an agent reads the local log and ships it. A log management platform receives the events, converts each line into a common structure — this is called parsing or normalization: the same field name for "source address" whatever the device that wrote it — indexes the events so that a search over millions of lines returns in seconds, and stores them for the retention period.

Examples: rsyslog and syslog-ng are collectors present on most Linux systems; GraylogVirusTotal check, OpenSearchVirusTotal check with a shipper such as Fluent Bit, and the Elastic StackVirusTotal check are platforms. This category detects nothing by itself: it creates the searchable memory that every other function depends on. On the Val-des-Pins network, FW-01, SW-01, SW-02 and NAS-01 send syslog; SRV-FILE-01 and PC-ACCT-01 send Windows events through an agent; MAIL-CLOUD offers an audit log that is exported through the provider's interface. Three limits to remember. First, a log contains only what the audit policy was configured to record — if object-access auditing is off on the file server, no tool in any category will show who opened the accounting share. Second, a computer that is compromised can have its local logs altered or deleted, which is precisely why logs are copied to a central store as soon as they are written. Third, every device must have the correct time from an NTP (Network Time Protocol) source; otherwise events from different devices cannot be placed in order, and a sequence such as "logon, then file access, then connection to the Internet" cannot be reconstructed.

Category 2 — Network traffic capture and analysis tools (evidence: packets and flow records)

These tools observe the network itself. A packet analyzer (also called a protocol analyzer) such as WiresharkVirusTotal check or tcpdumpVirusTotal check reads every frame on an interface and decodes its layers — Ethernet, IP (Internet Protocol), TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) or UDP (User Datagram Protocol), and the application protocol. A computer normally receives only the frames addressed to it; to see the traffic of other machines, the switch must copy it. A SPAN (Switched Port Analyzer) port, also called a mirror port, is a switch port configured to receive a copy of the frames from selected ports or VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network)s; the sensor is connected to that port. A network TAP (Test Access Point) is a small hardware device inserted into a cable that passes a copy of the signal to the sensor without depending on the switch. Full packet capture stores every packet: it is the most complete evidence and the most expensive in disk space. An office link of 100 megabits per second that is busy 20 % of the time carries 2.5 MB (megabyte) per second, which is about 216 GB (gigabyte) per day — more than the entire 200 GB (gigabyte) envelope of Val-des-Pins. This arithmetic is why Class 7 deferred full packet capture of the office.

Flow records are the economical alternative. Routers, firewalls and some switches export one record per conversation in the NetFlow format (created by Cisco), in the standard IPFIX (IP Flow Information Export) format defined in RFC (Request for Comments) 7011, or in sFlow, which samples one packet in N. A flow collector such as ntopngVirusTotal check or nfdump stores and displays them; a firewall's own connection log is the same kind of evidence written as events. Flow data answers "who talked to whom, when, on which port, and how much" for months, in a small fraction of the space of packets, and it works even when the content is encrypted. On the Val-des-Pins network, a sensor on a SPAN (Switched Port Analyzer) port of SW-01 observes the office; the connection records of FW-01 observe the Internet boundary; CNC-PC-01, on which no software may be installed, is observed only in this way. Two limits: content protected by TLS (Transport Layer Security) is not readable, and a capture on a shared network records other people's communications — section 7.2 of the Legal Notice allows capture only in the lab and only on Designated Targets; section 184 of the Criminal Code applies elsewhere.

Category 3 — Availability and performance monitoring tools (evidence: metrics)

These tools answer two questions: is the device reachable, and how loaded is it? The usual method is polling: the monitoring server asks each device at a fixed interval, for example every 60 seconds. An ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) echo request — the ping command — answers "reachable or not" and gives the round-trip time. SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) lets the server read counters from a device's MIB (Management Information Base), a structured database of values inside the device, each value identified by an OID (Object Identifier); a switch exposes in this way the number of bytes and errors on each port, its processor load and the state of each interface. SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) version 3 adds authentication and encryption and is the version to use; versions 1 and 2c send a community string — in effect a password — in clear text on the network. A device can also send an SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) trap on its own initiative when something happens, for example when a link goes down, without waiting to be polled. For operating-system metrics such as disk usage, memory and the state of services, an agent (the Zabbix agent, for example) is installed on the computer.

Examples: ZabbixVirusTotal check, Nagios CoreVirusTotal check, LibreNMSVirusTotal check, PrometheusVirusTotal check with GrafanaVirusTotal check for dashboards; PRTG from Paessler is a commercial example. Outputs are status maps — green for reachable, red for down — graphs over time, and threshold alerts such as "disk above 90 %" or "no answer for 3 minutes". On the Val-des-Pins network, FW-01, SW-01, SW-02, SRV-FILE-01 and NAS-01 are polled; the needs "service availability" and "disk usage" written in Class 6 belong here. Limits: a metric tells you that something is wrong, rarely what; polling is itself network traffic and must be sized with the constraints of Class 6; and a device that is green — reachable — can be fully compromised. Availability tools are the first thing a small company installs, and the last thing that detects an intrusion.

Category 4 — Intrusion detection and prevention systems (evidence: traffic or host activity compared with rules)

An IDS (Intrusion Detection System) examines traffic or host activity for signs of attack and raises an alert; an IPS (Intrusion Prevention System) is placed in-line — the traffic passes through it — and can also block. A NIDS (Network-based Intrusion Detection System) such as SuricataVirusTotal check or SnortVirusTotal check reads packets from a SPAN (Switched Port Analyzer) port or a TAP (Test Access Point) and compares them with signatures: rules that describe known malicious patterns, for example a request that matches a known exploit or a connection to a known command-and-control address. Rule sets are updated frequently; keeping them current is part of Lesson 3.3. ZeekVirusTotal check is an NSM (Network Security Monitoring) tool of a different kind: instead of matching signatures, it produces structured logs of every connection, every DNS (Domain Name System) request, every TLS (Transport Layer Security) certificate seen on the wire — it turns packets into events, which makes it a bridge between category 2 and category 1. A HIDS (Host-based Intrusion Detection System) such as WazuhVirusTotal check or OSSEC (an open-source host-based intrusion detection system) runs as an agent and examines the host's logs, the integrity of its files and signs of hidden software.

Two detection methods exist and both will return in Topic 5. Signature-based detection recognizes known patterns: it is precise and it is blind to an attack that has never been described. Anomaly-based detection (baseline-based) flags a deviation from measured normal activity: it can catch new behaviour and it produces more false alarms. The reference document is NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) SP (Special Publication) 800-94, Guide to Intrusion Detection and Prevention Systems (NIST CSRCVirusTotal check). On the Val-des-Pins network, the NIDS (Network-based Intrusion Detection System) runs on the same sensor as category 2, fed by the SPAN (Switched Port Analyzer) port of SW-01; the HIDS (Host-based Intrusion Detection System) agent runs on SRV-FILE-01 and PC-ACCT-01. Limits: encrypted traffic hides the content from a NIDS (Network-based Intrusion Detection System); false positives consume the technician's 60 minutes; rules must be updated; and an IPS (Intrusion Prevention System) that blocks legitimate traffic is a defensive change under section 7.4 of the Legal Notice — approved, with a window and a rollback, or not at all.

Category 5 — Endpoint monitoring tools (evidence: activity inside the computer)

These tools observe what happens inside a computer: the creation of a process with its command line and its parent process, the creation or modification of files, changes in the Windows registry, the network connections opened by each program, logons and the use of removable media. On Windows, SysmonVirusTotal check (System Monitor, a free Microsoft Sysinternals component) writes these detailed events into the Event Log, where a category-1 agent picks them up; on Linux, auditd plays the same role. EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response) products add response actions, such as isolating the computer from the network. FIM (File Integrity Monitoring) detects any change to a list of critical files, for example the configuration files of the file server. Antivirus and antimalware alerts are endpoint evidence too. On the Val-des-Pins network, endpoint monitoring goes on PC-ACCT-01 — the asset with the highest exposure to people and media in Class 7 — and on SRV-FILE-01; it cannot go on CNC-PC-01, because the vendor's support contract forbids installing software on that machine. Limits: one agent per computer means one installation and one update cycle per computer; agents consume processor time and memory; and they collect detailed data about how a person uses a computer, which makes data minimization under Law 25 and section 6.7 of the Legal Notice a design decision, not an afterthought.

Category 6 — Configuration and vulnerability assessment tools (evidence: state at one moment)

These tools observe state, not activity. A vulnerability scanner such as Greenbone (OpenVAS)VirusTotal check, or Nessus as a commercial example, connects to each system, identifies the services and versions that answer, and compares them with a database of known weaknesses identified by CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) numbers. A configuration assessment tool such as CIS-CAT, or any SCAP (Security Content Automation Protocol)-compatible tool, compares the settings of a system with a published benchmark from the CISVirusTotal check. Both run on a schedule — weekly or monthly — and both are active: they send packets, create load, and appear in the target's logs exactly as the first phase of an attack would. In this course you only need to recognize the category; scanning is taught in 420-3C1-DW Managing Vulnerabilities, and section 7.6 of the Legal Notice applies: even inside the lab, only Designated Targets. For Val-des-Pins, a monthly state check of SRV-FILE-01 and FW-01 is a later addition, not part of Lab 2.

Category 7 — Correlation, alerting and visualization platforms (evidence: everything from the other six)

A SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) receives events, flow records, metrics and alerts from the other categories, normalizes them, stores them and correlates them. A correlation rule connects several observations that are harmless one by one: five failed logons followed by one successful logon, from the same address, within ten minutes, is a pattern that no single event shows. The platform raises alerts with a severity, offers dashboards and reports, and often includes case management, a record of who examined which alert and what was concluded — the deliverable of Lesson 5.4. Examples: WazuhVirusTotal check combines agents, a manager and a dashboard in one open-source platform; Security OnionVirusTotal check is a distribution that assembles Suricata, Zeek, host agents and a search platform on one installation; Elastic SecurityVirusTotal check and Graylog offer alerting on top of log management; Splunk and the cloud SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) services of the large providers are the commercial examples.

A SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) is only as useful as the sources feeding it. For a company of 22 employees, the platform is justified from the moment three or more sources exist — Val-des-Pins reaches that point at Lab 2, with the firewall, the file server and the accounting workstation. Limits: commercial platforms are often priced by data volume, which turns every additional source into a monthly cost; the platform requires skills and, above all, tuning — the reduction of false alarms that occupies Topic 6.

3.1.4 Six ways to classify any tool

Categories say what a tool observes. Six additional axes say how it works, and each axis has consequences for cost, for load on the network, for privacy and for the skills required. Agent-based tools install software on the monitored machine and see inside it; agentless tools observe from outside through syslog, SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol), a SPAN (Switched Port Analyzer) port or an API (Application Programming Interface) — and they are the only option for a machine such as CNC-PC-01. Passive tools receive logs or a copy of the traffic and add no packets to the network; active tools send requests — pings, SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) polls, scans — which create load and are recorded in the target's logs. Continuous tools observe all the time, with a detection delay of seconds to minutes; scheduled tools run at set times and show the state at that moment. Signature-based tools match known patterns; baseline-based tools flag deviation from measured normal activity. Open-source tools publish their code and cost nothing to license, with support from a community or, optionally, from a paid vendor; commercial tools are licensed, often per device or per volume of data, with vendor support included. On-premises tools run on the organization's own hardware or lab machine and the data stays inside; cloud (SaaS (Software as a Service)) tools run on the provider's servers, the data leaves the site, and a subscription is paid. Figure 3.1.2 places the six axes side by side with the Val-des-Pins choices.

3.1.5 How the categories combine

A monitoring need is covered when at least one category observes the evidence the need requires; a plan is covered when every included need is. This is the coverage map: assets in rows, categories in columns, a mark in each cell where a need is served. Two consequences follow. A critical asset should be observed by two independent categories — for example, the file server by its own event log (category 1) and by the flow records of the switch (category 2) — so that the failure or the compromise of one source does not blind the technician. And one machine can host several categories: the monitoring server of Val-des-Pins, MON-01, is a single lab virtual machine that runs the log collector, the availability poller, the network sensor and the SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) console at the same time (Figure 3.1.1). Categories are functions, not boxes.

Slide 30Real-life example 3.1 — The tool-category coverage map of Ébénisterie Val-des-Pins Inc.

Task. Take every asset kept in the Class 7 monitoring plan, take each of its monitoring needs, identify the kind of evidence the need requires, and map that evidence to one of the seven categories. Produce a coverage map (assets in rows, categories in columns) and a spreadsheet listing every need with its category and its collection method (agent or agentless).

How it relates to this lesson. The map is Lesson 3.1 applied to a real plan: it turns the "what to observe" of Topic 2 into the "which category of tool" of Topic 3, and it shows why a small network needs several categories on one machine. Where it goes next. The coverage map is Section 1 of the Tool Selection Record you will hand in with Lab 2 (Saturday, October 3); the categories serving the Tier 1 assets decide which tool you install first in Lab 2; and in Lab 3 (Friday, October 16) the same map is reused for Lesson 6.3, improving monitoring coverage, where every empty cell becomes a candidate improvement.

Slide 31The situation

Monday, September 28, 2026. The part-time technician of Val-des-Pins has one hour before the shop opens. On the desk: the network map from Lab 1, the register of monitoring needs from Class 6, and the ordered plan from Class 7 — FW-01, MAIL-CLOUD, PC-ACCT-01, SW-01, SRV-FILE-01, CNC-PC-01 (connection records only), SW-02, and NAS-01 added by a documented override; AP-01 and the office workstations deferred to the October 16 review. The owner has asked one question: "Which software do we need to buy?" The technician's answer must begin with categories, not with brand names, because the plan lists twenty-three needs of five different kinds of evidence.

The technician proceeds need by need. "Administrator logins on the firewall" is an event written in syslog: category 1. "Device reachable" is a metric obtained by polling: category 3. "Execution of a program never seen before on PC-ACCT-01" is host activity that only an agent can see: category 5. "Copy of office traffic" is packets from the SPAN (Switched Port Analyzer) port of SW-01: category 2, and the same copy feeds the intrusion detection rules of category 4. When the technician reaches CNC-PC-01, the second need — "logon events on the machine PC (Personal Computer)" — requires a Windows event log, which requires an agent, which the vendor contract forbids: the need is recorded as a gap and the asset stays observed agentlessly through the connection records of FW-01. At the end, the map shows eight assets, five categories in use, and no category-6 or category-7 cell yet — the SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) is the console on MON-01 that will receive everything, and the scanner is a later, lab-only activity.

Deliverables of the example (reused in Lab 2 and Lab 3)

  • vdp_tool_category_map.csv — one row per need: asset, tier, need, evidence, category code and name, collection method, status (covered or gap). Table 3.1.B below is this file.
  • The coverage matrix (the visualization of the program, downloadable as an image) and one paragraph stating which categories serve the Tier 1 assets: C1, C3 and C5 — therefore the first tool of Lab 2 must collect logs, poll availability and manage endpoint agents, or be a platform that does all three.
  • The list of gaps with the constraint that causes each one — here, one gap, CNC-PC-01, vendor contract.

Slide 32Program 3.1 — class8_tool_categories.py (Python 3, no external modules)

What the program does. It holds the seven categories, a dictionary that maps each kind of evidence to its category, and the Class 7 plan with the needs of each asset. It walks through the plan need by need, looks up the category, checks the agent constraint, fills the coverage matrix, counts the assets served by each category, reports the gaps, and writes the spreadsheet vdp_tool_category_map.csv.

How it relates to the lesson. The dictionary EVIDENCE_TO_CATEGORY is Lesson 3.1.2 written as data; the loop is the coverage principle of 3.1.5; the agent check is axis 1 of 3.1.4. The simulator below executes the same logic step by step in the page: press Start, then Pause at any step to discuss it; Step advances one line; Restart begins again. The trace window shows every step; the matrix on the right fills in as the program runs. Legal reminder: the program processes fictional data only (section 6.4, "keep it fictional").

114# Define the function that builds the coverage map so that the steps can be followed one by one.
115def build_coverage_map(plan):
116    # Prepare the matrix: one row per asset, one True/False cell per category, all False at the start.
117    matrix = {item["asset"]: {code: False for code in CATEGORIES} for item in plan}
118    # Prepare the list of CSV rows, one per need.
119    rows = []
120    # Prepare the list of gaps: needs that cannot be covered because of a constraint.
121    gaps = []
122    # Walk through the assets in the order of the plan.
123    for item in plan:
124        # Read the asset code once, for readability.
125        asset = item["asset"]
126        # Walk through the needs of this asset.
127        for need, evidence in item["needs"]:
128            # Look up the category that produces this kind of evidence.
129            category = EVIDENCE_TO_CATEGORY[evidence]
130            # Decide whether this evidence needs an agent on the machine.
131            needs_agent = evidence in AGENT_REQUIRED
132            # Check the constraint: an agent-based need on a machine where no agent is allowed is a gap.
133            if needs_agent and not item["agent_allowed"]:
134                # Keep the gap for the report; the need is not marked as covered.
135                gaps.append((asset, need, evidence))
136                # Record the row anyway, with a note, so that the spreadsheet is complete.
137                rows.append([asset, item["tier"], need, evidence, category, CATEGORIES[category],
138                             "agent", "GAP - no agent allowed on this machine (vendor contract)"])
139                # Go to the next need without marking coverage.
140                continue
141            # Mark the cell (asset, category) as covered.
142            matrix[asset][category] = True
143            # Record the row for the spreadsheet.
144            rows.append([asset, item["tier"], need, evidence, category, CATEGORIES[category],
145                         "agent" if needs_agent else "agentless", "covered"])
146            # Print the mapping so that the class can follow the reasoning line by line.
147            print(f"{asset:12} need: {need[:46]:46} evidence: {evidence:26} -> {category}")
148    # Give back the three results.
149    return matrix, rows, gaps
150 
151 
152# Define the function that summarizes the matrix per category.
153def summarize(matrix):
154    # Count, for each category, how many assets it serves.
155    counts = {code: sum(1 for asset in matrix if matrix[asset][code]) for code in CATEGORIES}
156    # Sort the categories from the most used to the least used.
157    ordered = sorted(counts.items(), key=lambda pair: pair[1], reverse=True)
158    # Print a header line for the summary.
159    print("\nAssets served per category:")
160    # Print one line per category with a small bar made of '#' characters.
161    for code, count in ordered:
162        print(f"  {code} {CATEGORIES[code]:46} {count:2} {'#' * count}")
163    # Return the ordered list for the caller.
164    return ordered
165 
166 
167# Define the function that writes the spreadsheet.
168def write_csv(rows, path):
169    # Open the file for writing; newline='' is required by the csv module on Windows.
170    with open(path, "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as handle:
171        # Create a writer object.
172        writer = csv.writer(handle)
173        # Write the header row.
174        writer.writerow(["Asset", "Tier", "Monitoring need", "Evidence", "Category code",
175                         "Category", "Collection", "Status"])
176        # Write all the rows.
177        writer.writerows(rows)
178    # Tell the technician where the file is.
179    print(f"\nSpreadsheet written: {path}")
180 
181 
182# Run the program only when the file is executed directly (not when it is imported).
183if __name__ == "__main__":
184    # Build the map.
185    matrix, rows, gaps = build_coverage_map(PLAN)
186    # Summarize it.
187    ordered = summarize(matrix)
188    # Determine the minimum set of categories that the plan requires (every category used at least once).
189    required = [code for code, count in ordered if count > 0]
190    # Print the minimum set.
191    print("\nCategories required by the plan:", ", ".join(required))
192    # Determine which categories serve the Tier 1 assets - they decide the FIRST tool to install in Lab 2.
193    tier1 = {code for item in PLAN if item["tier"] == 1 for code in CATEGORIES if matrix[item["asset"]][code]}
194    # Print the Tier 1 categories in code order.
195    print("Categories serving Tier 1 assets (first tool for Lab 2):", ", ".join(sorted(tier1)))
196    # Print the gaps, if any.
197    for asset, need, evidence in gaps:
198        print(f"GAP: {asset} - '{need}' needs {evidence} (agent) but no agent is allowed; observe agentlessly.")
199    # Write the spreadsheet next to the program.
200    write_csv(rows, "vdp_tool_category_map.csv")

Step-by-step explanation of Program 3.1

    
    
      
  1. Header, import and constants. The header comments state the task and the legal frame; the program needs only the standard csv module. CATEGORIES is the reference table of the lesson in dictionary form: the key is the code C1 to C7, the value is the name.
    2. 
      
  2. Evidence dictionary. EVIDENCE_TO_CATEGORY lists every kind of evidence a need can require — "syslog", "SNMP metric", "packet capture", "host activity" and so on — and the category that produces it. Changing a mapping here is the only thing you would edit to adopt a different taxonomy.
    3. 
      
  3. Agent constraint. AGENT_REQUIRED names the two kinds of evidence that can only be obtained with software installed on the machine: the Windows event log and host activity. Each asset in the plan carries agent_allowed, which is False for network devices, for the cloud service and for CNC-PC-01.
    4. 
      
  4. The plan. PLAN is the Class 7 order. Every asset has its tier and a list of pairs (need, evidence). Twenty-three needs in total.
    5. 
      
  5. Building the map. build_coverage_map() creates the empty matrix, then for each asset and each need it looks up the category, decides whether an agent is needed, and either records a gap (agent needed, agent not allowed) or marks the cell and prints the mapping. The continue statement skips the marking when a gap is found — the need is written to the spreadsheet with the status "GAP" but the matrix cell stays empty.
    6. 
      
  6. Summary. summarize() counts, for each category, how many assets have at least one covered need, sorts the categories from the most used to the least used, and prints a small bar of # characters — the same information as the bar counters in the visualization.
    7. 
      
  7. Results for Lab 2. The main block computes the categories required by the whole plan (C1, C3, C5, C2, C4) and the categories serving the Tier 1 assets (C1, C3, C5), prints the gap for CNC-PC-01, and writes the spreadsheet with write_csv(). The Tier 1 set is the specification of the first tool for Lab 2.

Slide 35Flash cards — Lesson 3.1 (click a card to reveal the answer)

  



  

    
1The three functions of a monitoring toolclick to flip

    
Collection (obtain observations from a data source), storage (keep them for the retention period), evaluation and presentation (compare with rules, thresholds or a baseline; show and alert).

  





  

    
2Agent versus sensorclick to flip

    
An agent is a program installed on the monitored computer that reads local data (logs, processes, files). A sensor observes network traffic from outside the computer, fed by a SPAN port or a TAP; nothing is installed on the target.

  





  

    
3The five kinds of evidenceclick to flip

    
Events (logs), metrics (sampled values), flow records (conversation summaries), packets (complete transmitted units) and states (configuration or weaknesses at one moment). Two further categories examine or combine them: intrusion detection and SIEM.

  





  

    
4SPAN port and TAPclick to flip

    
A SPAN (mirror) port is a switch port configured to receive a copy of the frames of selected ports or VLANs so that a sensor can see them. A TAP is a hardware device inserted into a cable that passes a copy to the sensor without depending on the switch.

  





  

    
5SIEMclick to flip

    
Security Information and Event Management: a platform that receives events, flow records, metrics and alerts from the other categories, normalizes and stores them, correlates them with rules (five failed logons then one success within ten minutes) and raises alerts with a severity. Justified from about three sources.

Lesson 3.2 · 24 minutes · Slides 38–58 of the deck
Selecting the right tool for a given need

    
  

  

    


  
  

3.2.1 The need comes first


A tool is selected to satisfy a stated need; a need is never rewritten to fit a tool that someone already likes. Lesson 2.4 gave you the template of a monitoring need; in this lesson it becomes a testable sentence with six elements: the asset observed, the evidence required (event, metric, flow record, packet or state — Lesson 3.1.2), the behaviour to detect, the acceptable delay between the behaviour and the alert, the recipient of the alert, and the retention of the data. The first need of Val-des-Pins for Lab 2 reads: "N-01: collect the security event logs of FW-01, SRV-FILE-01, PC-ACCT-01 and SW-01, keep them 90 days within 200 GB (gigabyte), and alert the technician by e-mail within 5 minutes when one of the predefined suspicious behaviours occurs." Every word of that sentence can be verified during the pilot, and that is the point: a need that cannot be tested cannot be used to choose.


Two distinctions structure the rest of the lesson. A requirement is something the need or a constraint imposes — "reads Windows event logs" — while a preference is something the technician would like — "a dark-themed dashboard". Requirements decide; preferences only break ties. Among the requirements, a knock-out criterion (also called a must-have) is a condition whose failure removes a candidate from consideration whatever its other qualities, while a weighted criterion is a quality that candidates satisfy more or less and that is scored. Confusing the two produces the classic error of a spreadsheet in which an excellent but unaffordable product "wins".

  




  
  

3.2.2 The constraints that filter the list


Lesson 2.3 identified the organizational and operational constraints of the network; here they become filters. Budget and licence: Val-des-Pins has no licence budget for monitoring, which keeps the long list to open-source software and to editions that are free for this use; "free" must be verified on the publisher's site, because community editions often limit the volume of data or the number of devices. People and skills: one part-time technician with 60 minutes per day; a platform that needs two hours of daily care is a platform that will stop being used. Hardware capacity: the monitoring server is one lab virtual machine with 8 GB (gigabyte) of RAM (Random-Access Memory) and 200 GB (gigabyte) of disk; the publisher's documented minimum decides whether the product can even be installed. Network impact: agents consume processor time on the monitored computers, pollers create traffic, and a SPAN (Switched Port Analyzer) port occupies a switch port — Lesson 2.3 asked you to keep monitoring below a measurable fraction of the network's capacity. Operating systems and sources: the tool must read Windows 11 event logs, the syslog of Linux and of the network devices, and the audit log export of the cloud e-mail service; a product that reads only one of the three does not cover the need. Contracts: CNC-PC-01 must remain agentless. Law and privacy: the tool must allow data minimization and a retention limit, because every capture is personal information under section 7.2 of the Legal Notice and Québec's Law 25. Documentation and support: the technician will search the documentation more often than a help desk. Maintenance: updates, rule sets and storage growth — the subject of Lesson 3.3. Exit: a tool that can be removed without loss, and whose data can be exported, protects the organization from being locked in.

  




  
  

3.2.3 The selection procedure in seven steps


Step 1 — State the need with its six elements, as above. Step 2 — List the constraints that apply to this need; most come from Lesson 2.3 and from the envelope of Lesson 2.5. Step 3 — Build the long list: candidates from the category that the need requires (Lesson 3.1); a need for events is not served by a packet analyzer, however good the analyzer. Four to eight candidates are enough. Step 4 — Apply the knock-out filter: for each candidate, verify each must-have from the publisher's documentation, not from marketing pages; one failure removes the candidate, and the reason is written down. The survivors form the short list.


Step 5 — Weighted scoring. Before looking at any candidate, list the weighted criteria and give each a weight, with the weights summing to 100; then give each short-listed candidate a score from 0 to 5 on each criterion, with one sentence of justification per score. The weighted total is the sum over the criteria of weight × score, divided by the maximum score, 5; with weights summing to 100, the total is a percentage. Fixing the weights first prevents the most common bias, which is to adjust the weights until the preferred product wins. This tool of decision-making is called a decision matrix; it is used far beyond cybersecurity, and its value lies in the written justifications more than in the arithmetic. Step 6 — Pilot: install the first-ranked candidate in the Authorized Lab Environment for a fixed time, measure what the need says — installation time, memory and disk used per day, whether each predefined suspicious behaviour raises an alert within the stated delay — and keep a snapshot to roll back. If the pilot fails, the next short-listed candidate is piloted. Step 7 — Decision record: one page stating the need, the constraints, the candidates, the knock-outs, the scores, the choice, the alternatives rejected and why, the date, and a review date. The record is what you will show an auditor, a successor, or the owner who asks "why this one?" six months later — and it is the starting point of Lesson 6.5, recommending tools and improvements.

  




  
  

3.2.4 Frequent selection errors


    
  
  • Choosing by popularity. The most downloaded tool is not the one that fits the need of a 22-person company; popularity says something about documentation and community (a legitimate weighted criterion), nothing about fit.
    • 
  
  • Resource mismatch. A platform whose documented minimum is 16 GB (gigabyte) of RAM (Random-Access Memory) on an 8 GB (gigabyte) lab machine will not run; the constraint is checked in the knock-out step, not discovered during the pilot.
    • 
  
  • Ignoring licence terms. "Free" editions with a daily data limit or a device limit stop working, or become illegal to use, when the limit is exceeded — section 6.6 of the Legal Notice makes licence compliance your responsibility.
    • 
  
  • Forgetting the technician's time. A tool is not chosen for the day of installation but for the ninety days that follow; maintenance effort is a criterion with its own weight.
    • 
  
  • Collecting more than the need. Full packet capture "because it is more complete" exceeds the storage envelope, and it collects the content of people's communications that the need did not ask for; privacy and storage both point to the minimum.
    • 
  
  • No rollback. A pilot without a snapshot turns a failed test into a broken lab.
    • 
  
  • Wrong category. An availability monitor that "also has a log item" is not a log management platform; the need's evidence decides the category before any comparison starts.
    • 
  
  • No decision record. An undocumented choice cannot be reviewed, defended or improved; it will be re-argued from zero at every change of technician.
    • 


  




  
  

3.2.5 Four mini-cases


Case A — "I want to know within five minutes if the file server stops answering." Evidence: a metric. Category: availability monitoring (C3), polling SRV-FILE-01 every 60 seconds with ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) and reading its disk counters with SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) version 3 or a light agent; candidates Zabbix, Nagios Core, LibreNMS. A packet analyzer would show the absence of traffic only to someone watching it; an IDS (Intrusion Detection System) has nothing to compare.


Case B — "Alert me when someone fails to log on to PC-ACCT-01 five times in ten minutes." Evidence: Windows Security events 4625 (failed logon) and 4624 (successful logon). Category: log collection (C1) with a correlation rule (C7). Candidates: Wazuh, Graylog with an event shipper, Elastic Security. The rule is the predefined suspicious behaviour of Lesson 3.5; the audit policy must record failed logons, or the tool sees nothing.


Case C — "Show me which internal computer sends the most data to the Internet each day." Evidence: flow records or the connection records of FW-01. Category: traffic analysis (C2) with a flow collector such as ntopng, or a report on the firewall's connection log (C1). Full packet capture would answer the question at a hundred times the storage cost and would record content nobody asked for.


Case D — "Observe CNC-PC-01 without installing anything on it." Evidence: its connections. Category: agentless observation — the connection records of FW-01 (C1) and, if needed, the SPAN (Switched Port Analyzer) port of SW-02 feeding the sensor (C2 and C4). The constraint (vendor contract) removes every agent-based candidate at the knock-out step, whatever its score.

Slide 49Real-life example 3.2 — Choosing the first tool for Lab 2 with a weighted decision matrix

    
Task. For need N-01 of Val-des-Pins, apply the seven-step procedure: state the need, list the constraints, build a long list of six candidates, apply four knock-out criteria, score the survivors on seven weighted criteria, and write the decision record with a pilot plan and a review date. Produce the decision matrix as a spreadsheet and the decision record as a one-page table.

    
How it relates to this lesson. The example is Lesson 3.2.3 executed on the coverage map of Lesson 3.1: the categories serving the Tier 1 assets (C1, C3, C5) define the long list; the constraints of 3.2.2 define the knock-outs; the weighted criteria of Table 3.2.A define the score. Where it goes next. The decision matrix and the decision record are Sections 2 and 3 of the Tool Selection Record handed in with Lab 2 (October 3); the chosen tool is the one you install and configure in Lab 2; the review date, October 16, is Lab 3, where Lesson 6.5 asks you to recommend tools and improvements starting from this record.

  

  

    
Slide 50The situation

    
Same Monday, one hour later. The coverage map says that the first tool must collect logs from Windows and from network devices, manage endpoint agents, and raise alerts; availability polling can be a second tool later. The technician writes need N-01 on one line, then the six constraints, then a long list of six candidates: two open-source platforms designed for logs and alerts (Wazuh and Graylog Open), one open-source network-security distribution (Security Onion), one availability monitor (Zabbix), one packet analyzer (Wireshark), and one commercial cloud SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) subscription — the last three are on the list on purpose, to show that the knock-out step removes them for reasons that no score could compensate.

    
The technician reads each publisher's documentation and fills in four facts per candidate: category, licence cost, documented minimum memory, and e-mail alerting. The filter removes Security Onion (documented minimum memory above the 8 GB (gigabyte) lab machine), Zabbix (category C3, not C1), Wireshark (category C2, no central store, no alerting) and the cloud SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) (monthly cost). Two survivors are scored on the seven criteria, each score with one sentence of justification; the totals are 89.0 % for Wazuh and 69.0 % for Graylog Open. The decision record names Wazuh for the pilot of Lab 2, keeps Graylog Open as the runner-up, fixes the review date, and states the rollback: a snapshot of MON-01 taken before installation. Nothing has been installed yet; the choice is on paper, verifiable, and dated.

Slide 51Program 3.2 — class8_tool_selection.py (Python 3, no external modules)

    
What the program does. It holds the need, the constraints, four knock-out tests written as small functions, seven weighted criteria with their weights, and six candidates with their facts and scores. It applies the knock-outs and prints each verdict, computes the weighted total of each survivor, ranks them, prints the decision record, and writes the spreadsheet vdp_tool_selection_matrix.csv.

    
How it relates to the lesson. The four knock-outs are step 4 of Lesson 3.2.3; the formula in weighted_total() is step 5; decision_record() is step 7; step 6, the pilot, is Lab 2 itself. The simulator below runs the same steps in the page: the knock-out board turns each candidate green or red, then the bars of the survivors grow criterion by criterion, then the ranking and the record appear. Pause on any step to discuss the justification of a score. Fictional data only (section 6.4).

1# Cyber.SoHo - 420-1C1-DW Preventative Monitoring - Class 8 (Sat, Sept 26, 2026) - Lesson 3.2
2# Program: class8_tool_selection.py
3# Task: choose the FIRST monitoring tool for Lab 2 at Ebenisterie Val-des-Pins Inc. with a
4#       weighted decision matrix: (1) state the need, (2) list the constraints, (3) long list of
5#       candidates, (4) knock-out filter, (5) weighted scoring, (6) pilot plan, (7) decision record.
6# Educational material - Cyber.SoHo / Asen Grozdanov. (c) 2026 Cyber.SoHo. All rights reserved.
7# Run only in an Authorized Lab Environment (Legal Notice v2.0, sections 6.4 and 7.2). Fictional data.
8# The candidate facts below were entered by the technician from each publisher's documentation
9# as read in September 2026 - always re-check the current documentation before you rely on them.
10 
11# Import the csv module to write the matrix as a spreadsheet.
12import csv
13 
14# State the need in one testable sentence (asset, evidence, behaviour, delay, recipient, retention).
15NEED = ("N-01: collect the security event logs of FW-01, SRV-FILE-01, PC-ACCT-01 and SW-01, keep them "
16        "90 days within 200 GB, and alert the technician by e-mail within 5 minutes when one of the "
17        "predefined suspicious behaviours occurs.")
18 
19# List the constraints that come from Class 6 (2.3) and Class 7 (2.5).
20CONSTRAINTS = [
21    "zero licence budget (open-source or free for this use)",
22    "one part-time technician, 60 minutes per day for monitoring",
23    "one lab virtual machine with 8 GB of RAM and 200 GB of disk",
24    "sources: Windows 11 event logs, Linux and network-device syslog, cloud audit log export",
25    "no agent on CNC-PC-01 (vendor contract) - agentless observation only",
26    "lab environment only, fictional data (Legal Notice v2.0, sections 6.4 and 7.2)",
27]
28 
29# Define the knock-out (must-have) criteria; a candidate that fails one is removed before scoring.
30KNOCKOUTS = [
31    # K1: the tool must belong to the category the need requires (C1 log management + alerting).
32    ("K1", "belongs to category C1/C7 (log collection with rule-based alerting)", lambda t: t["category"] in ("C1", "C7")),
33    # K2: the licence must cost nothing for this use.
34    ("K2", "zero licence cost", lambda t: t["licence_cost"] == 0),
35    # K3: the documented minimum memory must fit the 8 GB lab virtual machine.
36    ("K3", "documented minimum RAM fits the 8 GB lab VM", lambda t: t["ram_min_gb"] <= 8),
37    # K4: the tool must be able to send an e-mail alert when a rule matches.
38    ("K4", "can send an e-mail alert when a rule matches", lambda t: t["alerting"]),
39]
40 
41# Define the weighted criteria; the weights are decided BEFORE scoring and add up to 100.
42CRITERIA = [
43    ("W1", "Fit to the need: log collection plus rule-based alerts", 25),
44    ("W2", "Ease of installation and daily use for a beginner", 20),
45    ("W3", "Resource demand inside the lab VM (memory, disk)", 15),
46    ("W4", "Documentation and community support", 10),
47    ("W5", "Daily maintenance effort (updates, rules, storage)", 10),
48    ("W6", "Coverage: Windows, Linux, network devices, cloud logs", 10),
49    ("W7", "Growth: can add flow records or an IDS later", 10),
50]
51 
52# The long list of candidates with the facts used by the knock-outs and the scores (0 to 5) per criterion.
53CANDIDATES = [
54    # Wazuh: open-source platform combining agents, a manager and a dashboard.
55    {"name": "Wazuh", "category": "C7", "licence_cost": 0, "ram_min_gb": 4, "alerting": True,
56     "scores": {"W1": 5, "W2": 4, "W3": 4, "W4": 5, "W5": 4, "W6": 5, "W7": 4}},
57    # Graylog (open edition): log management platform with alerting; needs a separate log shipper.
58    {"name": "Graylog Open", "category": "C1", "licence_cost": 0, "ram_min_gb": 4, "alerting": True,
59     "scores": {"W1": 4, "W2": 3, "W3": 3, "W4": 4, "W5": 3, "W6": 4, "W7": 3}},
60    # Security Onion: complete network-security-monitoring distribution; documented minimum RAM is high.
61    {"name": "Security Onion", "category": "C7", "licence_cost": 0, "ram_min_gb": 16, "alerting": True,
62     "scores": {"W1": 5, "W2": 2, "W3": 1, "W4": 4, "W5": 2, "W6": 4, "W7": 5}},
63    # Zabbix: availability and performance monitoring (category C3), not a log platform.
64    {"name": "Zabbix", "category": "C3", "licence_cost": 0, "ram_min_gb": 2, "alerting": True,
65     "scores": {"W1": 1, "W2": 3, "W3": 5, "W4": 5, "W5": 4, "W6": 3, "W7": 2}},
66    # Wireshark: packet analyzer (category C2); no central storage, no alerting.
67    {"name": "Wireshark", "category": "C2", "licence_cost": 0, "ram_min_gb": 1, "alerting": False,
68     "scores": {"W1": 0, "W2": 3, "W3": 5, "W4": 5, "W5": 3, "W6": 2, "W7": 1}},
69    # A commercial cloud SIEM subscription: fits the need but has a monthly cost.
70    {"name": "Cloud SIEM (commercial)", "category": "C7", "licence_cost": 250, "ram_min_gb": 0, "alerting": True,
71     "scores": {"W1": 5, "W2": 4, "W3": 5, "W4": 4, "W5": 5, "W6": 5, "W7": 5}},
72]
73 
74 
75# Define the function that applies the knock-out filter.
76def apply_knockouts(candidates):
77    # Keep the survivors here.
78    shortlist = []
79    # Examine each candidate in turn.
80    for tool in candidates:
81        # Evaluate every knock-out and keep the codes of the ones that fail.
82        failed = [code for code, text, test in KNOCKOUTS if not test(tool)]
83        # Print the verdict for the class.
84        print(f"{tool['name']:26} knock-outs failed: {', '.join(failed) if failed else 'none - short-listed'}")
85        # A candidate with no failure joins the short list.
86        if not failed:
87            shortlist.append(tool)
88    # Return the short list.
89    return shortlist
90 
91 
92# Define the function that computes the weighted total of one candidate.
93def weighted_total(tool):
94    # Sum weight x score over the criteria.
95    total = sum(weight * tool["scores"][code] for code, text, weight in CRITERIA)
96    # Divide by the maximum score (5) so that the result is a percentage when the weights sum to 100.
97    return total / 5
98 
99 
100# Define the function that scores and ranks the short list.
101def rank(shortlist):
102    # Compute the total of every short-listed candidate.
103    results = [(weighted_total(tool), tool) for tool in shortlist]
104    # Sort from the highest total to the lowest.
105    results.sort(key=lambda pair: pair[0], reverse=True)
106    # Print a header.
107    print("\nWeighted totals (weights sum to 100, scores 0-5, total = sum(weight x score) / 5):")
108    # Print each result with its contributions per criterion.
109    for total, tool in results:
110        contributions = "  ".join(f"{code}:{weight * tool['scores'][code] / 5:.0f}" for code, text, weight in CRITERIA)
111        print(f"  {tool['name']:14} {total:5.1f} %   {contributions}")
112    # Return the ranked list.
113    return results
114 
115 
116# Define the function that writes the decision matrix as a spreadsheet.
117def write_matrix(candidates, results, path):
118    # Build a lookup of totals for the short-listed candidates.
119    totals = {tool["name"]: total for total, tool in results}
120    # Open the file for writing.
121    with open(path, "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as handle:
122        # Create the writer.
123        writer = csv.writer(handle)
124        # Write the header: candidate, category, knock-outs, one column per criterion, total.
125        writer.writerow(["Candidate", "Category", "K1", "K2", "K3", "K4"]
126                        + [f"{code} (w={weight})" for code, text, weight in CRITERIA] + ["Weighted total %"])
127        # Write one row per candidate.
128        for tool in candidates:
129            verdicts = ["pass" if test(tool) else "FAIL" for code, text, test in KNOCKOUTS]
130            scores = [tool["scores"][code] for code, text, weight in CRITERIA]
131            writer.writerow([tool["name"], tool["category"]] + verdicts + scores
132                            + [f"{totals[tool['name']]:.1f}" if tool["name"] in totals else "not scored"])
133    # Confirm the file.
134    print(f"\nDecision matrix written: {path}")
135 
136 
137# Define the function that prints the decision record.
138def decision_record(results):
139    # The winner is the first element of the ranked list.
140    best_total, best = results[0]
141    # The runner-up is the second, if there is one.
142    runner = results[1][1]["name"] if len(results) > 1 else "none"
143    # Print the record, section by section.
144    print("\nDECISION RECORD - Lab 2 first tool")
145    print(f"  Need ............ {NEED[:60]}...")
146    print(f"  Choice .......... {best['name']} ({best_total:.1f} %)")
147    print(f"  Runner-up ....... {runner}")
148    print("  Rejected ........ Security Onion (K3 RAM), Zabbix (K1 category), Wireshark (K1, K4), Cloud SIEM (K2 cost)")
149    print("  Pilot ........... install in the lab VM during Lab 2 (Oct 3); measure install time, RAM, disk per day;")
150    print("                    verify that the 5 predefined suspicious behaviours raise an alert; keep the snapshot to roll back")
151    print("  Review date ..... Oct 16, 2026 (Lab 3, Lesson 6.5 - recommendations)")
152 
153 
154# Run the program only when executed directly.
155if __name__ == "__main__":
156    # Print the need and the constraints first: the tool is chosen for them, not the reverse.
157    print("NEED:", NEED)
158    print("CONSTRAINTS:")
159    for line in CONSTRAINTS:
160        print("  -", line)
161    print()
162    # Step 4: knock-out filter.
163    shortlist = apply_knockouts(CANDIDATES)
164    # Step 5: weighted scoring and ranking.
165    results = rank(shortlist)
166    # Step 7: decision record (step 6, the pilot, happens in Lab 2).
167    decision_record(results)
168    # Write the spreadsheet next to the program.
169    write_matrix(CANDIDATES, results, "vdp_tool_selection_matrix.csv")


    

      

        
Slide 52Knock-out board and weighted totals — update as the program runs
          
          
        

        

      

      
Execution trace (every step is kept; scroll to review while paused)

    

  

  
  

    
Step-by-step explanation of Program 3.2

    
    
      
  1. Need and constraints. NEED is the one-sentence need N-01; CONSTRAINTS is the list from Lesson 3.2.2. The program prints both before anything else, because the order of the procedure is part of the method.
    2. 
      
  2. Knock-outs as functions. Each entry of KNOCKOUTS is a code, a sentence and a small anonymous function (lambda) that receives a candidate and returns True or False. K1 checks the category, K2 the licence cost, K3 the documented minimum memory against 8 GB, K4 the alerting capability.
    3. 
      
  3. Weighted criteria. CRITERIA lists seven codes, sentences and weights; the weights add up to 100 and are fixed before any candidate is examined.
    4. 
      
  4. Candidates. Each dictionary in CANDIDATES holds the four facts read by the knock-outs and a scores dictionary with one integer from 0 to 5 per criterion. In your Lab 2 record, each score carries one sentence of justification.
    5. 
      
  5. Filter. apply_knockouts() evaluates the four tests for each candidate, prints which ones fail, and keeps only the candidates with no failure in the short list.
    6. 
      
  6. Score and rank. weighted_total() computes the sum of weight × score over the seven criteria and divides by 5; rank() sorts the survivors from the highest to the lowest and prints the contribution of each criterion — the numbers drawn as coloured segments in the chart.
    7. 
      
  7. Record and spreadsheet. decision_record() prints the seven sections of the record, including the pilot plan and the review date; write_matrix() writes one row per candidate with the knock-out verdicts, the scores and the total or "not scored".
    8.

Slide 56Flash cards — Lesson 3.2 (click a card to reveal the answer)

  



  

    
1Need before toolclick to flip

    
A tool is selected to satisfy a stated, testable need with six elements: asset, evidence, behaviour to detect, acceptable delay, recipient of the alert, retention of the data.

  





  

    
2Knock-out (must-have) criterionclick to flip

    
A condition a candidate must satisfy to be scored at all; one failure removes it from the short list whatever its other qualities. The reason is written down. Examples: right category, zero licence cost, fits the lab VM, can alert.

  





  

    
3Weighted totalclick to flip

    
Sum over the criteria of (weight × score), divided by the maximum score. With weights summing to 100 and scores from 0 to 5, the total is a percentage. Weights are fixed before any score is given.

  





  

    
4Pilotclick to flip

    
A time-boxed installation in the Authorized Lab Environment that measures what the need says: installation time, memory and disk per day, and whether each predefined suspicious behaviour raises an alert within the stated delay. Snapshot before, rollback ready.

  





  

    
5Decision recordclick to flip

    
One page: need, constraints, candidates, knock-outs and reasons, scores, choice, alternatives rejected and why, date, review date. It is the starting point of Lesson 6.5 and of Lab 3.

Slides 59–60Recap and next steps
2 minutes

  


  
  

What to remember


    
  
  • A monitoring tool collects, stores, and evaluates or presents observations; it is built from agents, sensors, collectors and consoles.
    • 
  
  • Five kinds of evidence — events, metrics, flow records, packets, states — give the first five categories: log management (C1), traffic analysis (C2), availability and performance (C3), endpoint (C5), assessment (C6); intrusion detection (C4) examines the evidence for attack patterns, and the SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) (C7) correlates all of it.
    • 
  
  • Six axes classify any tool: agent-based or agentless, passive or active, continuous or scheduled, signature-based or baseline-based, open-source or commercial, on-premises or cloud.
    • 
  
  • A need is covered when at least one category observes the evidence it requires; the coverage map shows assets against categories, and one machine can host several categories.
    • 
  
  • Selection follows seven steps — need, constraints, long list, knock-out filter, weighted scoring, pilot, decision record — and the weights are fixed before any score is given.
    • 
  
  • Every tool named today is lawful in the lab on Designated Targets and an offence elsewhere; section 7.2 of the Legal Notice governs this course.
    •
